title: Four failures
hook: the mind fails four ways: false impressions, unsocial acts, false words, letting the body rule (Meditations 11.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was my child: Marcus's gentle answer to real harm. Your line was nine reminders.

Mechanics have a short list of the ways an engine goes wrong. Doctors have one for the body. Right after his nine reminders, Marcus wrote a short list of the ways a mind goes wrong: four of them, each with a sentence to say when you catch it. It reads like a small diagnostic card, the kind you could tape inside a kitchen cabinet.
screen: `AN ENGINE'S SHORT LIST.` → `THE MIND'S SHORT LIST.` → `FOUR FAILURES.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. There are four wrong turns of the ruling part of the mind, Marcus writes, to watch for constantly, and wipe out when you catch them, saying a line to each. Second, the first two. One: a thought you don't need. Say: this thought isn't necessary. The replay of an old argument, a worry you've already dealt with, a fantasy that goes nowhere. Two: something that pulls people apart. Say: this loosens the bonds between people. A cutting remark, a bit of gossip, a scheme that works for you by working against others. Third, words. Three: you're about to say something that isn't what you really think. Marcus counts it among the most absurd things there are, to speak not from your own mind. Flattery, a fake agreement, a performance. Fourth, the body. Four: the moment you catch yourself reproaching yourself, because the more divine part of you has been beaten and given way to the less honorable, mortal part, the body and its coarse pleasures. Notice what he calls it: a defeat of the ruling part, not a crime. So, four questions. Is this thought necessary? Does this act bind people or break them? Do I mean what I'm about to say? Who's in charge here, my reason or my appetite? He doesn't ask himself never to fail. He asks himself to catch it, wipe it out, and keep going.
screen: `FOUR WRONG TURNS TO WATCH FOR.` · `UNNEEDED THOUGHTS, UNSOCIAL ACTS.` · `WORDS YOU DON'T MEAN.` · `APPETITE IN CHARGE.` · then, large: `FOUR FAILURES.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day and find one of the four: a thought that kept looping, a word that pulled people apart, something you said and didn't mean, a moment your appetite ran the show. Don't scold yourself. Name it with Marcus's line, this isn't necessary, or this loosens the bonds, or this isn't my real mind, and let it go.
Four failures. Marcus's short list of the mind's wrong turns: needless thoughts, unsocial acts, words you don't mean, and appetite in charge. Today's word.
Your line: wipe it out. Four questions fit on one small card. Day six hundred twenty-five, done.

howItsDone: Stoic readers sometimes use Marcus's four checks as a quick daily review: needless thoughts, divisive acts, insincere words, and moments when appetite took over.

original.note: Greek: the ruling part, the mind's command center in Stoic thought. all four failures are its wrong turns.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of sins.
what it means: four ways the mind slips, each caught with a sentence and wiped out, not dwelt on.
what a scholar hears: hēgemonikon, the ruling part, is the Stoic name for the mind's command center; each failure is a turning of it away from its job.
recall: a man of keen natural talent

chat.says: My mind keeps replaying an old argument. What would Marcus do?
options: Catch it and say, this thought isn't necessary, then wipe it out and go on.
Replay it to the end, so he could finally find the words to win it.
Write a sharp reply to send later, so the other person knows he was right.
chat.meaning: In 11.19 Marcus lists four wrong turns of the mind, the first a thought you don't need, and says to catch it, name it, and wipe it out.

ruling part.meaning: Marcus's name for the mind's steering center

Marcus.meaning: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations to himself

nine reminders.meaning: Marcus's numbered list for meeting offense, from the entry before

notes: 11.19 paraphrased (Long: 'There are four principal aberrations of the superior faculty against which thou shouldst be constantly on thy guard... This thought is not necessary: this tends to destroy social union: this which thou art going to say comes not from the real thoughts... the fourth is when thou shalt reproach thyself for anything, for this is an evidence of the diviner part within thee being overpowered and yielding to the less honourable and to the perishable part, the body, and to its gross pleasures.').
